examples.title: Normal probability for one measurement
examples.prompt: Fasting blood glucose in healthy U.S. adults aged 30 to 50 is Normal with mean 95 mg/dL and SD 8.7 mg/dL, \(X\sim N(95,8.7^2)\). Find \(P(85\le X<115)\).

steps.say: X is fasting glucose, Normal with mean 95 mg/dL and SD 8.7 mg/dL.
The cutoff 85 sits 1.149 SDs below the mean and 115 sits 2.299 SDs above it. The table rows nearest these are 1.15 and 2.30.
The wanted area is the middle band between the two cutoffs, so it is the left area at 2.30 minus the left area at minus 1.15.
The table gives 0.9893 at 2.30 and 0.8749 at 1.15. Symmetry turns the negative cutoff into 0.1251, so the band holds 0.8642.
About 86.4 percent of healthy adults aged 30 to 50 have fasting glucose from 85 up to 115 mg/dL.

examples.title: Normal probability for a sample mean
examples.prompt: BUN in healthy U.S. adults aged 20 to 60 is Normal with mean 18 mg/100mL and SD 6 mg/100mL. What is the probability that the mean BUN in a sample of 16 healthy adults is between 15 and 24 mg/100mL?

steps.say: The sample mean of 16 adults is its own random variable. By the central limit theorem it is Normal and centered on the same mean of 18 mg/100mL.
The SD of 6 is divided by the square root of 16, so the SE is 1.5 mg/100mL.
Measured in SEs, 15 is 2 below the mean and 24 is 4 above it.
The table gives 1.0000 at 4.00 and 0.9773 at 2.00, so the chance the sample mean lands between 15 and 24 is 0.9773.

examples.title: Normal percentile
examples.prompt: For fasting blood glucose \(X\sim N(95,8.7^2)\) mg/dL, find the 25th percentile.

steps.say: The 25th percentile is the value with 25 percent of the area to its left.
The table starts at one half, so symmetry is used. The left area 0.75 falls between 0.7486 at 0.67 and 0.7517 at 0.68, so z is about 0.675 and the 25th percentile z is minus 0.675.
Going 0.675 SDs below the mean of 95 gives 89.13 mg/dL, so a quarter of these adults fall below about 89.13 mg/dL.
